source.title: Trust, Reciprocity, and Social History
source.authors: Joyce Berg, John Dickhaut, Kevin McCabe

studies.title: No history · Sending and returning money

fields.label: Question
fields.value: Do people entrust money to an anonymous partner, does the partner return it, and does knowing earlier participants’ choices matter?

fields.label: What the paper covers
fields.value: A one-shot investment game with separate no-history and social-history samples.

fields.label: Across the paper
fields.value: Many people sent money and some recipients returned it in anonymous one-shot exchanges. Providing prior outcomes changed some measures, with limited statistical precision.

fields.label: Expectation or comparison
fields.value: The baseline tests whether people send and return positive amounts despite the one-shot monetary prediction. The history treatment tests whether showing previous choices changes those decisions.

fields.label: Interpretation and limits
fields.value: Social history is information about earlier strangers, with no repeated interaction or partner reputation. Several comparisons are suggestive rather than strong statistical evidence.
fields.derivation: Scope of the published evidence and, where linked, differences from the Bench adaptation.

fields.label: Participants, procedure and measures
fields.value: Anonymous pairs act once. One person can send any portion of a ten-dollar endowment, and the amount sent is tripled. The counterpart decides how much of the tripled amount to return. The baseline includes 32 pairs.

fields.label: Result
fields.value: Many first movers sent positive amounts and some counterparts returned money despite having no material incentive to do so. Returns varied substantially.

fields.label: Participants, procedure and measures
fields.value: 28 additional pairs saw a report of earlier choices. The same sending and returning rules applied. Compare amounts sent, paybacks and their rank correlation across samples.

fields.label: Result
fields.value: In this arm the average sent was $5.36 and average payback $6.46. The send–payback rank correlation was 0.34; the reported resampling comparison for the change in correlation was p=.06.
